questions.topic: Mode imputation on a category
questions.learningObjective: Explain mode fill on a category
questions.stem: Why is mode imputation natural for a categorical column but not for a continuous one?

answer.exemplar: A category's mode is an actual observed level, so filling with it keeps values within the valid set. For a continuous variable the mode may be arbitrary or multimodal, and mean or median better represent the centre.

questions.explanation: The mode of a category is a real level, keeping filled values valid. For continuous data the mode is often ill-defined, so centre-based fills are preferred.
questions.hint: Mode is a real level for categories.

questions.topic: When dropping beats filling
questions.stem: When is dropping rows preferable to filling, from a validity standpoint?

options.text: When a fast result is needed.
When the dataset is large, regardless of missingness pattern.
When missingness is large or non-random, so filling would fabricate structure.
Always, because filling is never valid.

questions.explanation: Dropping is preferable when missingness is substantial or systematic, because filling would invent structure. Size or speed alone do not justify it.

questions.topic: A duplicate row and a duplicate key
questions.stem: A table has both exact duplicate rows and duplicate keys with conflicting values. What is the proper order of action?

options.text: Average all duplicate rows regardless of type.
options.misconception: applies one fix to both problems

options.text: Remove exact duplicates first, then ignore key collisions.
Drop the whole table and reload.
Resolve key collisions first, then remove exact duplicates.

questions.explanation: Key collisions corrupt joins and must be resolved first; exact duplicates are then safe to remove. Dropping everything or averaging is not justified.

questions.topic: What a declared column type commits you to
questions.learningObjective: Identify a type mismatch on load
questions.stem: A DECIMAL(10,2) column receives 123456789.012. What is the consequence?

options.text: It is stored exactly with no issue.
The value exceeds precision or scale and is rejected or rounded.
It becomes a string automatically.
The decimal point is dropped.

questions.explanation: DECIMAL(10,2) allows 10 total digits with 2 after the point, so 123456789.012 exceeds precision and scale. It must be rejected or rounded.

questions.topic: A number written on a label
questions.learningObjective: Recognise a phone number as categorical
questions.stem: A 'phone' column holds 10-digit numbers. Why should it not be numeric?

options.text: It should be a float for decimal safety.
It is too large to store as an integer.
It identifies a line, so sums and averages are meaningless.
It can be averaged to find a typical phone.
options.misconception: treats an identifier as a quantity

questions.explanation: A phone number is an identifier; arithmetic on it is meaningless. Storage size and type do not change that.
questions.hint: Does averaging phone numbers make sense?

questions.topic: Three marks of an absent value
questions.stem: A text column contains both null and empty strings. Are they equivalent for analysis?

options.text: Neither affects aggregates.
They are always identical in every system.
Empty string is missing, null is an error.
Not necessarily; empty string is a value, null is absence.

questions.explanation: An empty string is a present value of length zero, while null denotes absence. Systems may handle them differently in counts and filters.

questions.topic: When the mean is the right fill
questions.stem: Values 4, 6, 8 have two missing entries. After mean imputation, what is the column sum?
questions.explanation: Mean of 4,6,8 is 6; filling two gaps adds 12 to 18, giving 30. The arithmetic checks out.

questions.topic: When the median is the right fill
questions.stem: A housing price column is right-skewed. Which fill is most robust for missing entries?

options.text: Mean, because it uses all prices.
Median, because it resists the high-price tail.
Mode, because prices repeat often.
Zero, to be conservative.

questions.explanation: The median resists the high-price tail that skews the mean. Mode and zero are not defensible for continuous prices.

questions.topic: A duplicate row and a duplicate key
questions.stem: Why is a duplicate key more dangerous than a duplicate row?

options.text: It only affects display, not results.
It is easier to detect automatically.
It can join one record to many and corrupt aggregates.
Duplicate rows are always worse.

questions.explanation: A key collision fans out joins and corrupts aggregates. Duplicate rows are redundant but do not multiply records.

questions.topic: What a declared column type commits you to
questions.stem: A CSV loader declares 'age' as INTEGER but a row contains 'unknown'. What is the typical outcome?

options.text: The column becomes text for all rows.
It is stored as the string 'unknown' in an integer column.
It is converted to 0 automatically.
The row fails or the value becomes null, depending on strictness.

questions.explanation: A strict loader rejects or nulls the value; a lenient one may coerce. It is not silently stored as text or zero.

questions.topic: Three marks of an absent value
questions.stem: Before imputing, what must the analyst verify about a 0 in a numeric column?

options.text: That 0 can be ignored without checking.
That 0 always means missing in numeric data.
Whether 0 is a real measurement or a sentinel for missing.
That 0 should be converted to the mean immediately.

questions.explanation: Zero may be a legitimate value or a sentinel; the analyst must verify before treating it as missing. Assumptions either way risk corruption.

questions.topic: When the mean is the right fill
questions.stem: Which rule best guides the choice between mean and median imputation?

options.text: Use zero when unsure.
Always use the median because it is safer.
Always use the mean because it uses all data.
Use the mean for symmetric data and the median for skewed data.

questions.explanation: Matching the fill to the distribution's shape preserves the centre. Universal preferences for either centre or zero are wrong.
